title: RPO, RTO & Failover Drills
summary: RPO and RTO turn "we have backups" into numbers you can defend, and a failover drill is the only way to know those numbers are real rather than aspirational.

slides.markdown:
"We have backups" isn't a disaster-recovery plan — it's a claim with no number attached. **RPO** and **RTO** are the two numbers that make it concrete: how much data you can afford to lose, and how long you can afford to be down.

This topic covers how backup and restore strategy each drive one of those numbers, and the discipline most teams skip: actually rehearsing the failover before a real disaster forces you to find out whether it works.

slides.sectionTitle: RPO vs RTO: how much data you can lose vs how long you can be down
slides.markdown:
**RPO (Recovery Point Objective)** is the maximum acceptable amount of data loss, measured as time — an RPO of 5 minutes means that after a disaster, you can lose at most the last 5 minutes of writes. **RTO (Recovery Time Objective)** is the maximum acceptable downtime — an RTO of 1 hour means the system must be back up and serving within an hour of failure.

They're independent numbers answering different questions: RPO is about the backup's freshness, RTO is about the restore's speed. A system can have a tiny RPO (near-zero data loss, via continuous replication) but a large RTO (it takes hours to actually stand the replica up as primary), or the reverse.

Treat both as business decisions, not engineering defaults — a payments ledger needs an RPO close to zero; an internal analytics dashboard might tolerate losing an hour of data comfortably.

slides.sectionTitle: Diagram: RPO and RTO on a timeline around a failure
slides.markdown:
![Timeline with last backup, failure, and service restored points, marking the RPO gap before failure and the RTO gap after it](assets/rpo-rto-timeline.svg)

RPO looks backward from the failure to your last good copy of the data; RTO looks forward from the failure to the moment service is actually usable again. They sit on either side of the same failure point on the timeline, measuring two completely different things.

This is why a postmortem needs both numbers reported separately — "we lost 3 minutes of data and were down for 40 minutes" tells a very different story than either number alone.

assets.alt: Timeline with last backup, failure, and service restored points, marking the RPO gap before failure and the RTO gap after it

slides.markdown:
Your backup strategy sets your RPO ceiling. **Continuous replication** — streaming every write to a standby as it happens — gets RPO down to seconds, since the standby is nearly always current. **Periodic snapshots** — say, every 15 minutes — cap your RPO at that interval, since anything written since the last snapshot is lost. **Nightly backups** put RPO at up to 24 hours, acceptable only when losing a day of data is genuinely tolerable.

The trade-off is cost and complexity working in the opposite direction: continuous replication needs infrastructure that stays in sync in real time, which is more to build and monitor than a nightly cron job that dumps to storage.

Pick the strategy the business's RPO requirement actually demands — over-provisioning continuous replication for data nobody would miss after a day wastes engineering effort.

Your restore strategy sets your RTO. A **warm standby** — infrastructure already running, just not yet serving traffic — can be promoted to primary in minutes, since the hard part (provisioning, loading data) is already done. A **cold rebuild from backup** — spin up fresh infrastructure, restore data from a backup file, redirect traffic — takes far longer, often hours, since every step happens from scratch after the failure.

RTO and RPO aren't the same lever: a warm standby fed by nightly backups has a fast RTO (minutes to promote) but a poor RPO (up to a day of data loss), while a cold rebuild fed by continuous replication has a good RPO but a slow RTO, since standing up new infrastructure takes time regardless of how fresh the data is.

Designing for both numbers means choosing backup and restore strategy together, not assuming one good number implies the other.

slides.sectionTitle: Compare: backup/restore approaches by RPO, RTO, and cost
slides.markdown:
| Approach | RPO | RTO | Steady-state cost |
|---|---|---|---|
| Continuous replication + warm standby | Seconds | Minutes | Highest — full standby infra running always |
| Periodic snapshot + warm standby | Snapshot interval (e.g. 15 min) | Minutes | Medium — standby running, less replication overhead |
| Continuous replication + cold rebuild | Seconds | Hours | Medium — data pipeline running, no idle standby |
| Nightly backup + cold rebuild | Up to 24 hours | Hours | Lowest — no standby infra at all |

**How to decide:** find the business's actual RPO and RTO requirements first, then pick the cheapest row that meets both — paying for continuous replication and a warm standby when a 24-hour RPO and multi-hour RTO would genuinely be fine is money spent on a guarantee nobody asked for.

slides.sectionTitle: Running a failover drill: game days and chaos-style regional kill switches
slides.markdown:
A **failover drill** (often called a "game day") means deliberately failing a region — or simulating that failure with a controlled kill switch — and running the actual failover procedure, on purpose, before you need it for real. The goal is to measure your true RPO and RTO against the numbers on paper, and surface every manual step, missing permission, or stale runbook that a tabletop discussion would never catch.

Mature teams run these on a schedule, often against production with careful blast-radius limits, precisely because a drill against a staging environment doesn't exercise the real data volumes, real traffic patterns, or real on-call pressure that make failover hard. Chaos-engineering-style tooling that can kill a region on demand turns this from an occasional fire drill into a repeatable, low-drama exercise.

Every drill should end with the actual measured RTO and RPO written down and compared against the target — and the runbook fixed for whatever surprised you.

slides.sectionTitle: Pitfall: a disaster-recovery plan that's never been executed end to end
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "We have a documented failover runbook, so we're covered."

**Why it's wrong:** a runbook that's never been executed is a hypothesis, not a tested procedure. Real failovers routinely fail on things a document can't predict — a permission that expired, a script that was never updated after an infrastructure change, a step that assumes a person who left the team, or a dependency the runbook simply forgot to mention. The first time many teams discover their DR plan doesn't work is during an actual outage, which is the worst possible time to find out.

**Correct model:** a disaster-recovery plan only counts once it's been rehearsed end to end, ideally against production-like conditions, with the resulting RPO and RTO actually measured. Treat an unrehearsed runbook as unverified, not as a safety net you can rely on.

slides.sectionTitle: Real numbers: what RPO/RTO targets actually look like by industry
slides.markdown:
Concrete targets make the trade-off tangible. A **core banking ledger** typically targets RPO near **zero** (synchronous replication, no acceptable data loss) and RTO under **1 hour** — regulators often mandate this explicitly. An **e-commerce checkout** system might target RPO of **5 minutes** and RTO of **30–60 minutes** — losing a few minutes of orders in a true disaster is bad but survivable, and being down for an hour costs real revenue but isn't existential. An **internal analytics dashboard** might accept RPO of **24 hours** (yesterday's nightly backup) and RTO of a full business day, since nobody's making a real-time decision off it.

Notice the pattern: RPO and RTO targets track directly to *revenue and legal exposure per minute of the failure*, not to some universal best practice. A team defending a 4-hour RTO shouldn't be asked to justify it against a bank's 1-hour target — they should be asked to justify it against what an hour of their own downtime actually costs the business.

The interview-ready move: whenever you propose an RPO/RTO number, immediately attach the dollar or compliance cost that number is protecting against — an unattached number invites the wrong comparison.
